newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends up in US post strong US trade,output data.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends up in US post strong US trade,output data.

text.p: The dollar rose broadly, setting a near 31-month high against the mark, after strong overseas trade and brisk manufacturing activity data highlighted the U.S. economy's vigor.

Also aiding the dollar was further weakness in the mark versus most other European currencies. Over the past week, the mark not only sank to its lowest level against the dollar since June 1994, but hit more than four-year lows against the British pound and the Norwegian and Danish crowns.
A lacklustre German economy and expected bumpy ride towards European monetary convergence contrast sharply with current U.S. monetary stability and economic vitality, traders said.

"The trade and manufacturing numbers showed the United States economy is pulling ahead of Europe's. It is a natural pulling apart and is largely responsible for the dollar's drive higher," said Gabriel Grippo, chief dealer at Credit Agricole. Record U.S. exports held growth in the November trade deficit to 4.9 percent as the shortfall between exports and imports rose to $8.4 billion, well below expectations.

Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve said national industrial output grew a surprisingly strong 0.8 percent in December, the same as in November, as businesses operated at their fastest rates in more than a year.

The dollar peaked at 1.6190 marks in late trade after U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin repeated his assertion, stated twice earlier this week, that a strong dollar is in the U.S. interest and "will remain so".
His remark quashed market speculation that the Clinton administration was adverse to the dollar's new, lofty heights.
However, concerns lingered that Japanese monetary authorities may intervene in the foreign exchange markets to support the ailing yen.
Reported comments by an undisclosed source close to Japan's Ministry of Finance, saying Japan was unwilling to sell dollars, failed to dispel those fears, dealers said.

Against the yen, the dollar rose to 117.30/35 from 116.87/92 at Friday's open, buoyed by the November report which showed the United States' trade deficit with Japan shrank 12.9 percent to $4.32 billion.

The dollar closed at 1.6172/77 marks, a significant jump from Friday's 1.6020/30 open. In sympathy, the dollar touched a new 32-month high against the Swiss franc at 1.40 before closing at 1.3993/98 Swiss francs, up from 1.3845/55.

Highlighting German economic woes, a newspaper report on Friday said the government was increasingly concerned it would overshoot the strict budget deficit criteria needed to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
The Bonn Finance Ministry quickly retorted that the government still expected to meet the criteria.

But Handelsblatt, quoting unnamed officials, said a public spending freeze would be imposed this month and that Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt assumed there would be 4.2 million jobless in Germany in 1997 -- 200,000 above the previous target.
In other trading, the dollar fell to Canadian $1.3408/13 from C$1.3390/95 at the open. Sterling also fell to $1.6677/87 from $1.6745/50.
